papers.title: Automated aortoiliac calcification segmentation from arterial-phase computed tomography scans: development and validation
papers.abstract: Introduction: Arterial calcium is widely used as a biomarker for coronary artery disease but is underutilized in peripheral artery disease (PAD) due to challenges in automated measurement. We developed a fully automated deep-learning pipeline for aortoiliac calcium measurement from arterial-phase, contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT angiography (CTA). Methods: Two nnU-Net models perform aortoiliac arterial segmentation and identification of calcified voxels. We trained on 56 CT scans and validated on 106 scans by comparing the pipeline's calcium estimation from CTA against calcium burden on corresponding non-contrast phase CT within manually segmented arterial contours across radiodensity thresholds of 100-1,000 HU. Using the threshold maximizing correlation, we performed linear regression with five-fold cross-validation between pipeline-estimated and non-contrast calcium quantities, and risk reclassification analysis to compare pipeline-predicted and non-contrast-derived calcium burden quartiles using quadratically weighted kappa. Results: Non-contrast calcium voxels [≥]400 HU correlated best with CTA calcium burden (aortic Pearson r=0.952; iliofemoral Pearson r=0.955). Five-fold cross-validation of non-contrast calcium volume prediction ([≥]400 HU) from pipeline-estimated calcium burden demonstrated aggregated Pearson r>0.91 for all held-out folds in all regions. In risk reclassification analysis, quadratically weighted kappa for agreement of predicted and ground truth calcium quartile classification was k=0.88 for aorta, k=0.84 for bilateral iliofemoral arteries, and k=0.80 for combined. Conclusion: Aortoiliac calcium burden can be automatically quantified from CTA with excellent reproducibility against calcium voxels [≥]400 HU on non-contrast imaging. Quantification of this important biomarker expands opportunities for improved peripheral vascular disease diagnosis and risk prediction.

papers.title: Diffusion-based vertex-wise connectomics encodes individual differences in cognition, affect and pathology
papers.abstract: No two brains are wired alike, and much of a person's cognitive and clinical state is written in this individual variation, not in the group average. Structural connectomes, however, are typically read through group atlases that summarize connectivity into regional averages, leaving this individual signal untapped. We build a vertex-wise structural connectome, in which every cortical surface vertex is a node, and apply it across the Alzheimer's continuum. Using an independent dataset for methodological development and a multisite cohort of 317 participants from ADNI-4, we show that connection distance and organizational scale form a nested hierarchy, from a long-range backbone to fine, short-range structure. The individual fingerprint is strongest in medium- and short-range connections and becomes less distinctive as connectivity is pooled into atlas parcels. This individual structure can be recovered across spatial scales, although its fidelity depends on diffusion acquisition quality, with multishell data providing a more informative reference than single-shell data. In the aging brain, an individually referenced balance between short- and long-range connectivity is associated with episodic memory, cognitive reserve, depressive symptoms, and shared molecular pathology. While cognitive associations largely reflect diagnostic differences, associations with depressive symptoms and pathology burden remain detectable after adjustment for diagnosis. These findings show that individual structural connectomes retain clinically and biologically relevant variation that is not fully captured by diagnostic classification or group-level summaries.

papers.title: Pulsed X-Ray CT with Temporally Aware Reconstruction for Three-Dimensional Endovascular Guidance: Phantom Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Background: Endovascular fluoroscopy provides limited depth information. Projection-level x-ray pulsing and prior-image reconstruction could enable volumetric CT updates from sparse projection data. Purpose: To assess whether pulsed sparse-view CT combined with temporally aware reconstruction could accurately localize robotically manipulated endovascular devices in a phantom. Materials and Methods: We compared true pulsed acquisitions with matched retrospective sparsification (4--180 projections) in a modular phantom. Eight robotically generated device configurations in an anthropomorphic endovascular phantom were scanned with 1248 projections. Data were retrospectively sparsified to 6, 12, 24, 32, and 52 projections and reconstructed using filtered backprojection and a temporally aware prior-image method. Localization errors were measured relative to full-view filtered-backprojection measurements. Analyses were descriptive. Results: Mean CT number differences between true pulsed and matched retrospectively sparsified images were 4.8--6.2 Hounsfield units; corrected standard deviations were 27.5--29.9 Hounsfield units. Sparse-view filtered backprojection obscured device segments at 6 and 12 projections, whereas temporally aware reconstruction depicted both devices at all projection counts. At 6 projections, median centerline, guidewire-tip, and tip-to-vessel-wall errors were 0.82 mm (interquartile range, 0.10 mm), 0.71 mm (0.12 mm), and 0.03 mm (0.28 mm), respectively. All localization errors were below the 0.944-mm reconstructed voxel diagonal. Conclusion: True pulsed and matched retrospectively sparsified acquisitions showed similar CT numbers in a modular phantom. In an anthropomorphic endovascular phantom, temporally aware reconstruction of retrospectively sparsified data localized robotically manipulated devices within one reconstructed voxel diagonal.

papers.title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
papers.abstract: Purpose: To compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. Methods: This retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). We compared ModernBERT encoders fine-tuned on 20,444 reports, generative LLMs (gpt-6-luna, Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma), and typed decisions with Jev, the Decisions API and Qwen. Thresholds fixed on 450 development reports were applied unchanged externally. The primary metric was micro-F1; case-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for 11 internal comparisons. Results: Encoders were best internally (English 0.9853; radiologist-checked Japanese 0.9576) and exceeded Jev (differences 0.0367, 95% CI 0.0258-0.0484; 0.0336, 0.0215-0.0464). Externally, Jev (0.8844) lay within the encoder seed range (0.8656-0.9144), exceeded the three generative conditions tested externally (best 0.8564) and the Decisions API (0.8177), and had the smallest internal-to-external decrease (-0.0396). An encoder trained on 2,044 reports reached 0.8226 externally. Typed-versus-generated differences changed direction across models and test sets. At a fixed threshold of 0.5, Jev fell to 0.7753 externally. Conclusion: Fine-tuned encoders performed best with ample in-distribution labels. Although threshold-dependent, Jev, with thresholds fitted on only 450 labeled reports, fell within the encoder seed range externally and exceeded the generative LLMs and an encoder trained on 2,044 reports, making it an option when labels are scarce.

papers.title: Automated Gland MRI Radiomics for Predicting Time to Pathologic Progression during Prostate Cancer Active Surveillance
papers.abstract: Background: Repeated biopsies burden patients during prostate cancer active surveillance (AS). Existing MRI risk stratification tools avoiding biopsy remain limited by the difficulty of automated lesion segmentation. Purpose: To develop a model integrating gland MRI radiomics and clinicopathologic variables for predicting time to pathologic progression during prostate cancer AS. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-institution study included men with grade group 1 or favorable grade group 2 prostate cancer undergoing AS with fusion-targeted and systematic biopsy (2010-2025). Gland segmentation used nnU-Net; gland radiomic features were selected by LASSO-penalized survival regression to train an XGBoost accelerated failure time model. Comparator models were assessed by C-index, time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Kaplan-Meier, and decision curve analysis. Results: Of 522 men (median age, 64 years [IQR, 59-68]), 410 were assigned by site to development and 112 to internal testing. Gland segmentation Dice was 0.89 +/- 0.04. The C-index was higher for the gland radiomics model (0.77) than for clinicopathologic (0.68) and lesion radiomics (0.68) models (adjusted P [≤] .017), with the highest time-dependent AUC at 36 months (0.87 [95% CI: 0.78, 0.94]). Progression-free survival was lower in high-risk than low-risk groups (36 months, 63.9% vs 100%; 48 months, 55.4% vs 93.8%; log-rank P < .001). At a 0.25 risk threshold, 49.1% and 31.3% were low risk at 36 and 48 months (negative predictive value, 1.00; positive predictive value, 0.36). Conclusion: An automated gland radiomics model predicted time to pathologic progression during AS better than clinicopathologic and lesion-based models.

papers.title: Longitudinal Multimodality Imaging of Cardiovascular Abnormalities Following Definitive Chemoradiation for Lung Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cardiovascular complications following definitive chemoradiation therapy (CRT) for lung cancer are well recognized, but their longitudinal imaging manifestations remain incompletely characterized. We aimed to characterize cardiovascular abnormalities across multiple imaging modalities and electrocardiography during lung cancer survivorship. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included patients treated with definitive CRT between 2013 and 2025 who underwent baseline and follow-up cardiovascular assessments. Findings from computed tomography, echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging, coronary angiography, and electrocardiography were categorized into exploratory, literature-informed cardiovascular phenotype domains across five follow-up intervals. Longitudinal patterns were evaluated using generalized estimating equations (GEE). and exploratory associations with clinical cardiovascular adverse events (CVAEs) were assessed using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. Results: Eighty-six patients were included (mean age, 66, SD=9.1 years; 46 women). Baseline coronary, thoracic aortic, and valvular calcification were common, affecting 72%, 88%, and 50% of patients, respectively. During the first 0-6 months, reduced LV systolic function (53%), valvular dysfunction (35%), and pericardial effusion (19%) were observed. Pericardial effusion was observed in 37% at 1-2 years, while calcification progression and pulmonary vascular abnormalities were identified during later follow-up intervals. Longitudinal analyses suggested positive associations between successive follow-up categories and calcification progression (average OR, 4.30), pulmonary artery enlargement (OR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.10-2.02; P = 0.01), right-heart abnormalities (average OR, 1.65), and arrhythmia (OR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.30-2.38; P < 0.001). Exploratory associations between imaging abnormalities and clinical CVAEs were also observed. Conclusions: Longitudinal multimodality cardiovascular assessments identified heterogeneous cardiovascular abnormalities across follow-up intervals following definitive CRT for lung cancer. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate these observations.

papers.title: Generative Deep Learning Maps Brain Oxygen Metabolism and Its Age-Related Decline from Two Standard Noninvasive MRI Scans
papers.abstract: Purpose: To develop a generative deep learning model mapping the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) from minimal, contrast-free MRI. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study used 3-T MRI of healthy adults from one center (May 2015-June 2025). A conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) was trained to reproduce contrast-based analytical CMRO2 from progressively fewer quantitative MRI inputs (cerebral blood flow [CBF], T2*, T2, cerebral blood volume), T1-weighted MRI, or resting-state functional MRI. Models were trained on 54 participants and tested on 41 (25 women; mean age, 49 years +/- 23 [SD]), on calculation-task data, and, without retraining, on same-protocol (n = 24) and cross-vendor (n = 12) data. Agreement (r, mean absolute error [MAE]) was compared with the test-retest error of analytical CMRO2, and repeatability (n = 9) with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Results: A GAN using only CBF and T2* agreed with analytical CMRO2 as well as one adding T2 (r = 0.89 [95% CI: 0.88, 0.90] for both), with errors below the between-day test-retest error (median MAE, 38.1 vs 46.5 micromol/100 g/min); CBF alone, T1-weighted MRI, and functional MRI performed worse (P <= .004). It was as repeatable as analytical CMRO2 (median ICC, 0.87 for both), preserved task-evoked patterns (Dice, 0.78), agreed with same-protocol (r = 0.89) and, less, cross-vendor data (r = 0.81; P <= .001), and captured the age-related decline (6.8 vs analytical, 5.0 micromol/100 g/min per decade). Conclusion: Generative deep learning mapped brain oxygen metabolism from two contrast-free scans with repeatability comparable to the reference.

papers.title: Is Latin American brain anatomy "normal"? Construction and evaluation of a Chilean brain template
papers.abstract: Many neuroimaging processes use a brain reference anatomical template; the most widely used is the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template. Yet studies have shown that different populations exhibit different global brain features, and the use of a unique Canadian template may introduce biases in analyses for other populations. The purpose of this work is to construct a brain template that accurately represents our local population in Chile. In addition, our project explicitly addresses another pressing challenge: the limited availability of high-field MR scanners in Latin America. In this context, we will build our template using a 0.55T MR scanner, thus ensuring not only population specificity but also methodological alignment with the technological realities of our healthcare systems. Healthy volunteers (n = 76, ages 18-60) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Images were preprocessed and iteratively registered via rigid and non-linear steps to generate a Chilean template (CL76). Evaluation involved dimensional comparisons with Canadian, Indian, Chinese, and Korean templates. Deformation metrics were estimated for an additional 23 volunteers. The Chilean template measures 166 x 132 x 100 mm3, smaller than the Canadian one (179 x 137 x 118 mm3), and has distinct proportions, particularly the width/height ratio of 1.31 versus 1.16. Deformation of a test population onto CL76 was significantly lower (p = 0.010) and less variable than that of MNI152. The top deformed regions onto CL76 or onto MNI152 differed, confirming population specificity on the template. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first brain template generated in South America; however, we do not claim to represent the entire continent--only a specific population from Chile. This work highlights the need for broader representation across diverse populations, particularly to counterbalance the current over-representation of individuals from high-income countries with established research and imaging infrastructures.

papers.title: Lightweight and Explainable AI for Chest Radiograph Classification in Low-Resource Settings: Cross-Dataset Generalization, Grad-CAM Verification, and Uncertainty-Aware Referral
papers.abstract: Chest radiography is the most common imaging test worldwide, yet models trained on one hospital's data often fail elsewhere, a critical problem for low-resource hospitals that cannot collect large local datasets. This paper presents a lightweight, explainable framework for chest radiograph classification, trained and evaluated entirely on CPU with public data. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet-18 are trained on a 10,000-image subset of NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated without retraining on a paediatric pneumonia set, alongside a TorchXRayVision DenseNet121 pretrained baseline and a model trained directly on paediatric data. On the NIH test set (n = 2,500), the best single model reaches pneumonia AUC-ROC 0.738 and a two-model ensemble 0.742, while an adult-trained model falls to AUC 0.454 on paediatric images, and, symmetrically, a paediatric-trained model falls to 0.473 on adult NIH images. Pooling the adult and paediatric training sets into one binary pneumonia model changes the picture: a merged EfficientNet-B0 reaches AUC 0.951 (95% CI 0.932-0.967) on paediatric images, the first result whose whole 95% CI clears 0.90, and 0.675 on NIH images with zero sensitivity at threshold 0.5, while a merged ResNet-18 reaches 0.962 on paediatric and 0.606 on NIH images. Pooling fixes the catastrophic cross-domain failure but does not recover adult-only performance, and ensembling a merged model with a single-domain model adds nothing on either test set. Grad-CAM heatmaps are shown for true positives, false negatives and false positives, and Monte Carlo dropout referral raises answered-case accuracy from 0.889 to 0.948 on NIH data but not under domain shift. All results carry bootstrap confidence intervals, and the limits of a 22-positive NIH test set are stated plainly.

papers.title: Blood acceleration metric: A potential surrogate for fractional flow reserve to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenosis
papers.abstract: Purely morphological assessment of an arterial stenosis is not sufficient to adequately evaluate its functional significance. The metric of fractional flow reserve (FFR) is the gold standard for assessing coronary artery stenoses. However, the risks associated with catheterization and induction of hyperemia needed to measure FFR impede its application to cerebral vessels. Approaches based on a combination of computed tomography (CT) with computer simulations have been proposed to address this issue, yielding an estimate of fractional flow reserved (FFRCT). While promising, they are time-consuming and difficult to integrate into established clinical workflows. Here, we propose a new, easily derivable parameter termed the blood acceleration metric (BAM). It incorporates readily measurable morphological and hemodynamic features, such as minimum stenosis diameter and peak systolic velocity, to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenoses. Preliminary assessment on 27 mild to moderate stenoses indicates a strong negative correlation (R=-0.85) between BAM and FFRCT. BAM should be further evaluated as a potential surrogate for FFR and, thereby, as a possible predictor of stroke risk.

papers.title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. MethodsThis retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. ResultsOf 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. ConclusionManifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

papers.title: Anatomy-Aware 3D GAN with Local Mask Refinement for Brain MRI Inpainting
papers.abstract: Brain tumor MRI inpainting aims to synthesize plausible healthy-appearing tissue in regions removed from pathological scans. We present an anatomy-aware three-dimensional generative adversarial network for Task 4 of the BraTS 2026 challenge. The method combines mask-aware gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundary-aware refinement, and a local masked-region refiner, each adapted from established components in the image synthesis and inpainting literature. The model is trained with a two-stage objective that first emphasizes voxel-wise and structural reconstruction and then applies low-weight adversarial fine-tuning. On a deterministic local held-out split, the proposed method substantially improves over a simple 3D AutoEncoder baseline but does not surpass the challenges Pix2Pix3D baseline. On the official BraTS 2026 Task 4 evaluation server, the submitted model obtained a mean SSIM of 0.658 and a mean PSNR of 14.81 dB over 219 evaluated cases, lower than the local held-out figures. We report these results transparently, analyze likely contributing factors, and identify the controlled ablations (removal of the mirrored-context channel and of the two-stage schedule) required to isolate the contribution of each architectural component.

papers.title: Biomechanical characterization of head and neck tumors and corresponding lymph nodes for nodal assessment by ultrasound shear wave elastography and MR elastography
papers.abstract: BackgroundMalignant remodeling alters tissue mechanics, but biomechanical differences among primary head and neck tumors, benign cervical lymph nodes, and nodal metastases remain poorly characterized. We used in vivo and ex vivo ultrasound shear-wave elastography (USE) and ex vivo tabletop MR elastography (ttMRE) to compare stiffness, viscoelasticity, and spatial heterogeneity across these tissue groups and to assess cross-modal agreement. As a secondary objective, we explored whether primary-tumor biomechanics differed by pathological nodal status. MethodsEighteen patients - 17 with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and one with salivary duct carcinoma - underwent surgical resection. Target cervical lymph nodes were assessed by in vivo USE, and resected lymph nodes and primary tumors by ex vivo USE. Multifrequency ttMRE was successfully performed in 8 benign lymph nodes, 8 metastatic lymph nodes, and 13 primary tumors and yielded shear modulus , power-law exponent , and spatial heterogeneity metrics. Quantitative T1, T2, fat-fraction, and apparent-diffusion-coefficient (ADC) measurements were also performed. Group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests with Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc tests, paired comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and primary tumors from node-positive versus node-negative patients were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests. Diagnostic performance was summarized by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and cross-modal agreement by Spearman correlation. ResultsBy ttMRE, benign lymph nodes were softer than metastatic lymph nodes and primary tumors (median [IQR], 3.4 [3.1-8.9] vs 57.3 [26.2-102.4] vs 24.2 [13.2-37.6] kPa; p = 0.001) with more homogeneous texture as indicated by lower stiffness entropy (H(), 1.24 [1.05-1.30] vs 1.88 [1.71-2.27] vs 1.70 [1.56-1.78] nats; p = 0.002). Although the unpaired distributions of metastatic nodes and primary tumors overlapped, matched within-patient comparisons showed higher stiffness in primary tumors than in benign nodes and in metastatic nodes than in their corresponding primary tumors (n = 6 pairs per comparison; p = 0.031 for each). For discriminating metastatic from benign lymph nodes, AUC was 0.97 for ttMRE , 0.96 for in vivo USE, and 0.90 for ex vivo USE. By ttMRE, primary tumors from node-positive patients had lower stiffness than those from node-negative patients (12.1 [10.2-16.1] vs 30.1 [26.4-72.8] kPa; uncorrected p = 0.035), whereas ex vivo USE did not show differences (p = 0.415). ttMRE correlated with ex vivo USE ({rho} = 0.70, p < 0.001) and in vivo ({rho} = 0.69, p = 0.003). ConclusionIn our prospective cohort, tissue stiffness was the main biomechanical feature distinguishing benign from metastatic cervical lymph nodes. Furthermore, an association between lower primary-tumor stiffness and pathological nodal positivity was observed by MRE but not USE. Our findings establish a proof of concept for the biomechanical characterization of primary head and neck tumors and regional lymph nodes.

papers.title: Deep-learning body composition analysis of routine CT robust to scan range, slice order and contrast phase
papers.abstract: PurposeTo develop and validate a fully automated pipeline that measures skeletal muscle and adipose tissue at L1 and L3 on routine CT with varied scan ranges, slice orders and contrast phases, rejects levels outside the scan and converts measures to non-contrast equivalents. Materials and methodsThe pipeline (sarco) combines orientation detection, L1/L3 localisation with out-of-range rejection, U-Net segmentation, six-class contrast-phase estimation, phase-specific conversion to non-contrast-equivalent values and, as an auxiliary output, muscle and marrow age estimation. We evaluated it on five single-centre datasets (4986 series): agreement with radiologist-corrected labels using five-fold cross-fitting (2025 series), artificially truncated scans, contrast-enhanced series paired with non-contrast series of the same examination, and the prognostic value of fully automated measures in 2006 patients after curative cancer surgery. TotalSegmentator served as a comparator. ResultsOn held-out folds, L3 skeletal muscle area (SMA) agreed with the reference (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.983; bias +1.35 cm{superscript 2}). On truncated scans processed with cross-fitted localisation models, the chosen L3 slice was off by half a vertebra or more in 4.7-5.6% of volumes (TotalSegmentator 11.3-14.3%). Four-group phase accuracy was 0.949, exceeding TotalSegmentator in scans shorter than 400 mm (0.952-0.960 vs 0.643-0.668), and conversion reduced the root mean square error of L3 muscle attenuation against the same-examination non-contrast series from 7.96 to 2.81 HU. Combined age estimates had a mean absolute error of 6.5 years. Automatically measured low muscle mass increased the cross-validated Unos C of the baseline model by 0.034 (95% CI 0.009-0.053; cancer-specific survival) and 0.031 (0.016-0.048; overall survival), whereas converted L3 muscle attenuation added 0.012 (-0.005 to 0.024) for overall survival. ConclusionThe pipeline provides robust, contrast-phase-aware body composition measures from routine CT with varied scan ranges and reproduces known prognostic associations without manual input. Short abstractWe validated a fully automated pipeline for L1/L3 body composition on routine CT. It handled truncated scans, estimated the contrast phase, converted measures to non-contrast equivalents, agreed closely with radiologist-corrected labels and reproduced prognostic associations in 2006 surgical patients.

papers.title: Bootstrapping surgeon labeling campaigns with x0-diffusion: label-efficient vessel segmentation of catheter-based angiograms
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAssess which architecture is the most label-efficient for vessel segmentation of catheter-based angiograms, and whether a diffusion model trained with extreme data scarcity could serve as a scaffold for expert annotation. Materials and Methodsx0-diffusion, SAM, DeepLabV3, ResNet-UNet, ViT-DPT, and ResNet-ViT hybrid were compared at 16, 32, and 80 labeled images from the 500-image Dr-SAM dataset under 5x5-fold repeated cross-validation, using one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. A vascular surgeons annotation time, from scratch and when correcting x0-diffusion predictions, was also measured. ResultsAt 16 training images, x0-diffusion achieved the highest Dice (0.882) and IoU (0.795) of the six models, outperforming every competitor in all 25 paired runs on Dice, by 0.047 over zero-shot SAM and 0.226 over DeepLabV3. The advantage narrowed as labels increased: at 32 images x0-diffusion was not significantly different from the two strongest convolutional models, and at 80 images those models scored marginally higher (0.923 and 0.920 vs. 0.910). Correcting 16-image x0-diffusion predictions on five test angiograms averaged 11.1 surgeon-minutes per image versus 20.6 from scratch. DiscussionThe advantage of x0-diffusion is label efficiency, not peak accuracy, with the strongest convolutional models needing twice the labels to match it. It rarely fails where zero-shot SAM fails, so at the start of an annotation campaign, correcting its predicted masks could cut surgeon annotation time by an estimated 37 to 45%. ConclusionWith very few labels, x0-parameterized diffusion is the strongest vessel segmenter tested and a candidate scaffold for expert annotation. Layman SummarySegmenting vessels on an angiogram manually takes a vascular surgeon about twenty minutes per image. This study shows that an x0-diffusion model trained on only 16 angiograms draws outlines good enough to correct rather than redraw, which took the surgeon about half as long on five test images.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for pulmonary tuberculosis detection on chest X-ray images: A systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.

papers.title: Middle Temporal Gyrus Neurite Microstructure and Scam Susceptibility in Older Adults Without Dementia
papers.abstract: BackgroundFinancial exploitation is a prevalent public health concern among older adults, and emerging evidence links vulnerability to gray matter macrostructure and white matter microstructure, including within brain regions and networks implicated in early Alzheimers disease. Although diffusion tensor imaging is sensitive to age-related variation in brain microstructure, its scalar metrics cannot distinguish among the tissue properties contributing to observed differences. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) models distinct tissue compartments, yielding estimates of neurite density, dendritic complexity, and extracellular free water. MethodsThis study examined associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla imaging in 116 older adults without dementia. Neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and free-water fraction were quantified within seven a priori regions of interest linked to early Alzheimers disease. Multivariate regressions evaluated associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics, adjusting for age, sex, education, and global cognition, with multiple comparison correction within each metric. For significant regions, post-hoc hierarchical regression models tested whether NODDI metrics explained variance beyond regional cortical thickness, total gray matter, and total intracranial volume. ResultsGreater scam susceptibility was associated with higher NDI ({beta}=0.30, pFDR=.025) and lower ODI ({beta}=-0.28, pFDR=.044) in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG). No other regions survived correction. Additionally, MTG NDI and ODI explained variance beyond macrostructure measures. ConclusionsThese findings identify NODDI metrics as novel microstructural correlates of scam susceptibility beyond macrostructure, supporting investigation of their relevance to financial vulnerability in older age.

papers.title: Volumetric Analysis of the Deltoid Muscle From Neck-to-Knee Dixon MRI: A pilot population assessment of a posterior intramuscular injection target
papers.abstract: BackgroundDeltoid muscle volume varies across anatomical regions and population groups, with potential implications for intramuscular injection site selection. Evidence comparing middle and posterior deltoid volumes in vaccine-eligible populations is limited. PurposeTo compare middle and posterior deltoid muscle volumes by vaccine eligibility group, sex, and side. MethodsDeltoid muscles were manually segmented into anterior, middle and posterior regions in 43 UK Biobank Dixon MRI scans. A MONAI deep learning model trained on the annotations (Dice score = 0.78) segmented deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants, categorised by UK flu vaccination eligibility: A ([≥]65 years without risk conditions, n=1,760), B ([≥]65 with risk conditions, n=1,744), and C (<65 with risk conditions, n=1,735). Bilateral-average posterior and middle volumes were compared using a paired t-test. A linear mixed-effects model assessed posterior-middle differences by group, sex and side. ResultsMean age was 66.7 {+/-} 7.2 years and body mass index was 27.5 {+/-} 5.7 kg/m2 (mean {+/-} SD). Posterior deltoid volume exceeded the middle deltoid volume by 55.36 ml (95% CI, 54.14-56.58, p<0.0001). Posterior-middle differences were largest in Group A, followed by B and then C, greater in men, and greater on the right side (all p<0.0001). Mean segmentation-quality score was 4.27 {+/-} 0.73 on a five-point Likert scale and weighted inter-observer kappa was 0.583 (95% CI, 0.452 - 0.713). ConclusionsAmong individuals eligible for the UK flu immunisation, posterior deltoid volume was greater than middle deltoid volume. These findings support further anatomical assessment of the posterior deltoid as a potentially safer injection target. Key ResultsO_LIThe deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants from the UK Biobank matching UK annual influenza vaccination eligibility were segmented using a deep learning-based model, enabling precise volumetric quantification of the anterior, middle and posterior deltoids. C_LIO_LIThe posterior deltoid demonstrated a larger average muscle volume when compared to the middle volume across vaccine-eligible groups and sexes (p<0.0001). C_LIO_LIThese findings provide a comprehensive reference framework for deltoid assessment across different ages and genders, enhancing both research and clinical decision-making for IM injection site selection. C_LI Summary statementAutomated deltoid volumetry in a pilot UK Biobank cohort revealed greater posterior than middle deltoid volume, supporting further evaluation of the posterior deltoid for a potential alternative intramuscular vaccination site.

papers.title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
papers.abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression. ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period. ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

papers.title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. MethodsWe validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with [≥]1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. A per-category reclassification algorithm shifted patients along the existing Lung-RADS management ladder using a-priori score cutpoints. We evaluated a separately locked follow-up configuration on examinations with a prior scan. ResultsLungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88-0.95) and AUPRC 0.47 (0.35-0.61), outperforming Sybil ({Delta}AUROC 0.07; {Delta}AUPRC 0.18), diameter ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.34), and volume ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.38; all P<0.001). Against Lung-RADS v2022 scored ordinally on the weighted annotated subset, LungAI improved AUPRC ({Delta}AUPRC 0.31, P=0.003) but not AUROC ({Delta}AUROC 0.03, P=0.20). LungAI added discriminative information independent of diameter (likelihood-ratio {chi}2=161, P<10-36; {Delta}AUROC 0.10) and, on follow-up examinations, independent of delta diameter, volume doubling time, and new-nodule status ({chi}2=79, P<10-18). Integrated with Lung-RADS, LungAI reduced cancers on the slowest (12-month rescan) pathway by 46% (3.1[->]1.6 per 1,000 examinations) and benign biopsy referrals by 20% (32.7[->]26.2 per 1,000 examinations) at approximately unchanged total biopsy volume (51.0[->]50.1 per 1,000). Assuming full adherence to recommended follow-up, the combined approach yielded 25 months of net diagnostic lead time, an estimated net cost saving of [~]$2,200, and 6.5 fewer benign biopsies per 1,000 examinations; accounting for published adherence rates, it yielded 1.6 additional cancer diagnoses within 1 year per 1,000 examinations. ConclusionsLungAI contributes malignancy-risk information orthogonal to the size- and growth-based features underlying Lung-RADS and improves the allocation of screening patients across the existing management spectrum while potentially decreasing invasive procedures for benign lesions. Multi-site, multi-geography validation is required to demonstrate practical generalizability.

papers.title: WALRUS: Robust and Transferable Deep Learning for Water and Lipid Removal in 1H-MRSI
papers.abstract: Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI) enables non-invasive mapping of brain metabolism, but reliable quantification is challenged by residual water and extracranial lipid contamination. Recent work demonstrated that a deep learning model trained on simulated metabolite spectra combined with in vivo-derived water and lipid signals can outperform conventional nuisance-removal methods. However, this approach relied on heuristic simulation parameter distributions and a subject-specific L2-derived lipid estimate as an auxiliary network input, requiring subject-specific lipid masks and L2 processing during inference. Here, we introduce WALRUS (Water And Lipid Removal Using Spectral Learning), a fitting-consistent and empirically calibrated framework developed through a systematic evaluation of simulation realism, architectural priors, and network optimization. WALRUS uses the same metabolite basis as downstream spectral fitting and calibrates deliberately broadened simulation distributions from in vivo measurements. Controlled 7 T experiments demonstrate that empirical simulator calibration substantially improves nuisance removal and metabolite quantification compared with heuristic training distributions. With the optimized simulator, a capacity-matched comparison reveals no clear additional benefit from the L2-derived prior, allowing its removal and substantially simplifying inference. Further improvements are achieved with the final higher-capacity U-Net, while on-the-fly simulation improves generalization compared with training on a fixed synthetic dataset. The same framework was subsequently recalibrated and retrained at 3 T, where WALRUS outperformed conventional HLSVD+L2 processing on held-out data. Together, WALRUS combines these advances into an optimized framework that improves nuisance removal and downstream metabolite fitting, requires no subject-specific lipid segmentation or L2-derived auxiliary input during inference, and can be systematically adapted to different acquisition settings.

papers.title: Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings Found in Lung Cancer Screening: A Comparative Analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo compare LLM and prompting strategies for labeling Specific Incidental Findings (SIFs) occurring during lung cancer screening, in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsIn this retrospective study, 300 CT reports from a Dutch academic hospital were included between 19th March 2003 and 28th December 2020. GPT-5, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B-INST, MedGemma-4B-IT, a keyword-based search method, and a radiologist labelled the reports for the presence or absence of nine SIFs. The radiologists scores were the reference standard. Each LLM was evaluated with four different prompting strategies: two without Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and two with CoT (one zero shot, one few shot). The automated labelling methods were evaluated against the radiologist primarily using Cohens Kappa, and additionally sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores. ResultsGPT-5 achieved substantial or almost perfect agreement for seven out of nine SIFs: aortic valve disease, bronchiectasis, consolidation, coronary artery calcification, emphysema, abnormality in mediastinal lymph nodes, and thyroid abnormalities, with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.81 (0.70, 0.93), 0.97 (0.93, 1.00), 0.71 (0.62, 0.82), 0.92 (0.87, 0.96), 0.91 (0.84, 0.97), 0.71 (0.62, 0.80), and 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) respectively. For the remaining two SIFs, moderate LLM agreement was obtained with MedGemma-4B-IT and with GPT-4-Turbo with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.48 (0.40, 0.60), 0.42 (0.31, 0.58) for interstitial lung abnormalities and mediastinal mass respectively. The highest agreement was obtained with the non-CoT prompt strategies for most SIFs. ConclusionThis study demonstrated that LLMs can automatically label radiology reports with agreement ranging from almost perfect to moderate, but not one LLM - prompt combination achieved the highest agreement across all SIFs.

papers.title: MLX-Radiomics: accelerating standardized regional and voxel-wise radiomics for CT, PET and MRI
papers.abstract: BackgroundDifferences among radiomics implementations complicate cross-study comparisons, while voxel-wise feature extraction remains computationally demanding. We developed MLX-Radiomics to accelerate regional feature extraction and voxel-wise mapping while preserving agreement with standardized reference measurements. MethodsMLX-Radiomics implements 172 feature definitions from the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI), 16 extensions and the IBSI 2 image filters. We assessed agreement with IBSI reference data and evaluated numerical accuracy against independent double-precision and analytic calculations. In matched comparisons on Apple M1 Max and M5 Max systems, we used the IBSI reference CT to compare feature values, extraction time and memory use with PyRadiomics, MIRP and Flash-Radiomics, and feature values with FastRad. Separately, we compared the time required to generate voxel-wise feature maps for regions of up to 10.1 million voxels with published GPU results obtained on different hardware and images. We evaluated agreement with MIRP under published settings in a 51-patient cohort with CT, FDG PET and T1-weighted MRI. ResultsMLX-Radiomics agreed with all 2,160 IBSI reference measurements within the specified tolerances. With matching outputs, MLX-Radiomics was 2.66 to 7.27 times faster than PyRadiomics and MIRP for regional feature extraction and 198 to 218 times faster than PyRadiomics for voxel-wise mapping on a 243-voxel crop. It also outperformed the fastest Flash-Radiomics CPU configurations tested. On the M5 Max, generating 93 maps over 10.1 million voxels took 23.8 s. In the patient cohort, MLX-Radiomics and MIRP agreed on 98.0% of requested values. For tumors at the image edge, matching the libraries resampling rules substantially improved agreement. ConclusionsMLX-Radiomics provides standardized regional measurements and voxel-wise maps for CT, PET and MRI, with evidence of faster extraction limited to CT. It can support quantitative imaging research on relatively inexpensive hardware without requiring a separate GPU workstation.

papers.title: Assessing anterior shoulder instability: Reliability of the humeral head centralization test
authors: M. P. J. van den Bekerom
papers.abstract: BackgroundMotor control impairment of the rotator cuff muscles is reported to compromise the stability of the glenohumeral joint. However, an easily applicable, reliable parameter for quantifying anterior translation of the humeral head during active arm movements is lacking. Therefore, a novel (humeral head centralization) test was developed and evaluated. Study designCase-control study with reliability analysis (Level III). MethodsThis research project examined the shoulders of 25 patients with anterior shoulder instability and 25 asymptomatic controls. A physical therapist assessed humeral head translation in both groups during shoulder external rotation and elbow extension using ultrasound imaging. For test-retest and inter-rater reliability, the ultrasound assessment was repeated by the physical therapist and a radiologist after one week. Patients, the physical therapist, and the radiologist were blinded to the test results. In the evaluation of the difference in translation between the patients and controls, the Wilcoxon rank sum test was employed. The test-retest and inter-rater reliability were estimated using Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC2,1). ResultsIn patients, in active elbow extension, a significantly greater anterior translation of the humeral head was observed compared to participants in the asymptomatic group (p < .001). The test-retest reliability of the physical therapist demonstrated poor agreement for the external rotation movement (ICC2,1 0.32 (95% CI -0.08-0.63)) and moderate agreement for the extension movement of the elbow (ICC2,1 0.66 (95% CI 0.36-0.84)). The inter-rater reliability of the physical therapist and radiologist was moderate for both the external rotation (ICC2,1 0.51 (95% CI 0.16-0.75)) and elbow extension movements (ICC2,1 0.62 (95% CI 0.30-0.82)). ConclusionAlthough translation of the humeral head during active elbow extension movement was increased in patients compared to controls, this study found difficulties in reliably measuring anterior glenohumeral translation. Therefore, this novel test, in its current form, cannot be recommended for use in clinical practice or research.

papers.title: Deep Learning-based Framework for Rapid, Precise and Fully Automated Localization of Cochlea Landmarks in 3D CT Images
papers.abstract: Manual localization of anatomical landmarks within human cochlea structures in 3D computed tomography (CT) images is labor-intensive. However, despite progress in various studies on automatic localization methods, it remains challenging to jointly achieve rapid, precise, and fully automated landmark localization. Therefore, we propose a deep learning-based localization framework, called MEDICO-YOLO, which bridges speed and precision. It can automatically and simultaneously localize 6 human cochlea landmarks (apex, basal point, round window center of both left and right cochleae) in the full-resolution 3D CT images. The main contributions are: 1) MEDICO-YOLO learns from few manually annotated 3D CT images; 2) Within the framework, a 2D CNN-based network was developed to specifically localize cochlea landmarks in 3D single-scale medical CT images; 3) A novel loss function was designed; 4) The localization model achieved human expert-level precision while ensuring rapid inference. This study employed anonymized 3D pre-operative CT images (0.3 mm, covering the full head or temporal bone region). The evaluation involved comparing four models that were trained using 4 different training set sizes (n=4, 8, 12, 16). Each of them was evaluated on a distinct test set (n=16). The results show that the MEDICO-YOLO framework achieved strong localization performance by learning from few annotated 3D CT images. Trained on only 8 CT volumes, the model already attained a mean localization error of 1.30 mm (approximately 4 voxels). When trained on 16 CT volumes, the model achieved a mean error of 0.71 mm and a successful detection rate (SDR@3.0 mm) of 97.92%. Furthermore, on an Apple M1 laptop, the model achieved a real-time speed (32 ms) for inferencing each 2D slice (608 x 608) and an average latency of 25.43 s for inferencing the full 3D CT image (608 x 608 x 200, including post-processing). The complete methodology for the MEDICO-YOLO framework is presented in this article.

papers.title: Disability-relevant demyelination in multiple sclerosis: five-year evolution following diagnosis
papers.abstract: Improved understanding of how myelin damage contributes to disability in multiple sclerosis (MS) is needed to inform targeted therapeutic strategies and improve clinical trial platforms. Magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat) and T1 relaxometry provide in vivo quantitative MRI measures of myelin integrity, and may offer insights into disability-relevant pathology beyond inflammatory relapse. This longitudinal study explores the relationship between early demyelination and disability progression over the first five years following diagnosis. 62 people with relapsing-remitting (pwRR)MS ([≤] 6 months post-diagnosis, 48 female, mean age 38 years) underwent baseline and one-year MRI and Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) assessment. At five-year follow-up, 56/62 (90.3%) completed EDSS and 40/62 additionally completed MRI (64.5%). Disability progression was defined as an increase of [≥] 1.5, [≥] 1.0 or [≥] 0.5 points for a previous EDSS score of 0.05). One-to-five-year changes in MTsat were not associated with one-to-five-year disability progression (FDR-corrected p-values > 0.05). Neither baseline nor baseline-to-one-year MTsat changes predicted future disability progression. No exploratory analyses reached FDR-corrected statistical significance. We show for the first time that progressive NAWM and WML demyelination measured with MTsat is associated with early disability progression in recently diagnosed RRMS, independent of radiological inflammatory disease activity. Neither MTsat nor T1 are associated with longer-term progression over the subsequent four years. MTsat is sensitive to disability-relevant demyelination not visible on conventional MRI, indicates a potential early window of therapeutic opportunity in the year following diagnosis, and is a promising clinically applicable disease stratifier and surrogate endpoint for therapeutic trials.

papers.title: Brainstem functional connectivity integrates microbiome-gut-brain signals in healthy older adults: a cross-sectional evaluation and a randomised controlled probiotic trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundDespite increasing interest in the gut-brain axis, the role of the autonomic nervous system and the brainstem in human gut-brain signalling remain largely unknown. ObjectiveTo characterise resting state functional connectivity (FC) of the brainstem in healthy older adults and to examine its association with a variety of factors relevant to ageing and the gut-brain axis, and to assess if brainstem FC is altered by probiotic intervention. DesignRandomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial in 60-80-year-olds (55 women/28 men) with six-weeks Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus HN001 intervention in a non-encapsulated and microencapsulated formulation. Brainstem-optimised functional magnetic resonance imaging was performed before and after intervention. ResultsAt baseline, age correlated positively with FC of locus coeruleus (LC) and dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) with pre-/postcentral gyrus, as well as of periaqueductal gray (PAG) with temporal/supramarginal gyrus and planum temporale. FC of PAG with precuneus cortex and cingulate gyrus correlated with cognitive status and mood. Perceived stress correlated with FC between nucleus tractus solitarius and occipital cortex, angular/temporal gyrus. FC of DRN differed between men and women. All p<0.0063. Following probiotic intervention, a significant time*group interaction and main time effect were observed for FC of LC and ventral tegmental area. FC of both with occipital pole/cortex and cerebellum, and of LC with pre-/postcentral gyrus, superior parietal lobule, insular/opercular cortex, putamen, and planum polare showed within-group changes (non-encapsulated), no between-group differences were observed (all p<0.0056). ConclusionBrainstem-to-cortex FC at rest correlates with several phenotypic characteristics implicated in healthy ageing and may be modifiable by probiotic supplementation. KEY MESSAGESWhat is already known on this topic: Gut-derived signals, including those related to gut microbiota modulations, influence brain function. Whether and how those signals are transmitted via the autonomic nervous system and integrated via the brainstem remains largely unexplored in humans. What this study adds: Brainstem-to-cortex functional connectivity, originating especially from the periaqueductal gray and locus coeruleus, was associated with age, cognitive status and psychological symptoms; and functional connectivity especially of the locus coeruleus was also affected by probiotic intervention. How this study might affect research, practice or policy: From a human gut-brain perspective, imaging the brainstem may add to the understanding of the role of the autonomic nervous system in (patho-)physiological processes and modes-of-action of intervention effects. This may have clinical implications for conditions with disturbed signalling along this axis.

papers.title: The Para-ISS Dural Space Enhancement Sign: A Novel MRI Finding Independently Associated With Intracranial Atherosclerotic Burden
papers.abstract: BackgroundNo dural enhancement sign centered on the inferior sagittal sinus (ISS) has been characterized. We observed a frequent, previously undescribed finding--para-ISS dural space enhancement (PISE)--at the free inferior margin of the falx cerebri. ObjectiveTo define PISE, determine its detection rate in a large cross-sectional cohort, and characterize its correlates, in particular whether the pattern of association is compatible with an atherosclerosis-related dural mechanism. MethodsConsecutive contrast-enhanced intracranial vessel-wall MRI (VWI) examinations (May 2015-December 2025) were reviewed; 835 of 875 examinations were evaluable, corresponding to 811 patients. The first outcome-evaluable examination for each patient was used for all primary analyses. PISE was defined as dural enhancement strictly at the falx free margin adjacent to the ISS, exceeding the ISS vascular lumen. Forty-seven demographic, clinical-history, and imaging variables were tested univariately with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; multivariable logistic regression with patient-grouped 5-fold cross-validation was triangulated with LASSO and random forest. Dose-response across plaque grades was assessed with the Cochran-Armitage trend test, and circulation-specific associations were compared in models adjusted for age and sex (inter-reader Cohens {kappa}=0.93). ResultsPISE was detected in 609/811 patients (75.1%); detection rose from 50.0% ( 70 years; trend p=5.6x10-). The strongest univariate correlate was vulnerable intracranial plaque (OR=8.29, 95%CI 5.54-12.40). Detection increased across plaque grades 0/1/2 (38.7%[->]77.2%[->]90.3%; Z=11.09). Anterior-circulation plaque showed a stronger association than posterior-circulation plaque (OR=4.42 vs 2.76). Vulnerable plaque (OR=2.37), plaque grade (OR=2.84 per grade), age (OR=1.38 per SD), and inpatient status (OR=3.18) remained independently associated (patient-grouped cross-validated AUC=0.755). Moyamoya disease was inversely associated (OR=0.25). Findings were consistent across imputation and all-examination sensitivity analyses. ConclusionsPISE is a frequently detected novel dural enhancement sign whose independent, graded, anatomically concordant association with intracranial atherosclerotic burden supports an atherosclerosis-related dural mechanism and warrants prospective validation.

papers.title: Similar discrimination, different behaviour under synthetic occlusion: confidence and attribution reproducibility of deep learning models for intraoral ultrasonography
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo determine whether similar baseline discrimination conceals different responses to synthetic occlusion, whether loss of discrimination is accompanied by reduced confidence, and whether spatial attributions are reproducible in intraoral ultrasonography models. MethodsWe analysed 477 images from 40 healthy volunteers, using acquisition position to label superior and inferior subregions. Five architectures were evaluated across five training seeds on a subject-independent test set of 97 images from eight volunteers. Images underwent constant-intensity occlusion at boundaries spanning 30- 70% of image depth and an area-matched band-occlusion control. Attribution analyses assessed variation across seeds and class-activation methods and compared attribution-guided insertion with random insertion. ResultsSeed-mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.958 to 0.972, with rankings reversing across seeds. EfficientNet-B0 fell below 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions, compared with zero to two for the other architectures; the difference persisted with area-matched masking. Under 50% occlusion, its mean confidence on incorrect predictions rose to 0.989 and expected calibration error from 0.094 to 0.478. Between two inference runs, EfficientNet-B0s per-seed occluded AUCs differed by up to 0.161; seed means were 0.51-0.55 in both. Attribution patterns varied across seeds and methods. ConclusionsSimilar baseline discrimination concealed different occlusion responses, and loss of discrimination could coexist with high confidence. Attribution reproducibility provided a further constraint on interpretation. These findings concern the evaluated pipelines and synthetic masks; they do not establish anatomical mechanisms or clinical reliability. Advances in knowledgeJoint evaluation of perturbation sensitivity, confidence under perturbation and attribution reproducibility distinguished model behaviours that baseline discrimination alone did not reveal in intraoral ultrasonography.

papers.title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
papers.abstract: ObjectiveWe aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methodsWe gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybils performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. ResultsThe median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybils overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. ConclusionSybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings. Key pointsO_LIWe investigated whether AI risk stratification tools could identify the lowest-risk individuals undergoing lung cancer screening suitable for switching to a biennial screening schedule. C_LIO_LIIn our simulations, Sybil reduced follow-up screening load by at least 30% through switching the lowest-risk Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases to biennial screening without delayed cancer diagnoses. C_LIO_LIVery low-risk individuals, as predicted by AI algorithms, could potentially be placed on biennial screening schedules, reducing radiology department workload and freeing time for new patients. C_LI
